pr_title: feat(python)!: Allow all `DataType` objects to be instantiated
pr_body:
Closes #6163 

This went a lot more smoothly than I expected. This update should cause almost no friction with users.

###  Changes

* The following methods now return instantiated `DataType` objects, rather than a mix of classes/instances:
  * `Series.dtype`
  * `DataFrame.dtypes`
  * `LazyFrame.dtypes`
  * `DataFrame.schema`
  * `LazyFrame.schema`
  * `Series.struct.schema`
* Instantiating a DataType will now actually return an instantiated object, e.g. `Int8()` is no longer magically converted into an `Int8` _class_.
* Update the DataType class with default `__hash__`, `__eq__`, and `__repr__` methods. These are valid for 'simple' data types. 'Complex' data types like `Datetime` and `List` overwrite these defaults as they did before.
* Update conversion of DataTypes to/from Rust. Instantiated data types are now accepted and the returned data types are always instantiated.

Almost everything still works as before. The only thing really affected is the `is` operator:

**Before**

```pycon
>>> s = pl.Series([1, 2, 3], dtype=pl.Int8)
>>> s.dtype is pl.Int8
True
```

**After**

```pycon
>>> s.dtype is pl.Int8
False
```

Use the equality operator or `isinstance` instead:

```pycon
>>> s.dtype == pl.Int8
True
>>> isinstance(s.dtype, pl.Int8)
True
```

And users may have to update some of their type hints.

After this is merged, there can be a little more cleanup and refactoring to smooth things out further behind the scenes. But this should take care of the user-facing changes I intended to make.

issue_context.title: Polars datatypes should be instantiated
issue_context.body:
### Problem description

In Python, we have some advanced magic going on behind the scenes when it comes to handling Polars datatypes. This has some drawbacks that may lead to confusing behaviour for users:

```python
import polars as pl
from datetime import datetime

df = pl.DataFrame({'a': [1], 'b': [datetime(2023, 1, 1)]})

isinstance(df['a'].dtype, pl.Int64)  # False?
assert df['a'].dtype == pl.Int64  # Okay this works

isinstance(df['b'].dtype, pl.Datetime)  # True
assert df['b'].dtype == pl.Datetime  # This also works

map = {
    pl.Int64: 'x',
    pl.Datetime: 'y',
}

map[df['a'].dtype]  # Returns 'x'
map[df['b'].dtype]  # KeyError!
map[pl.Datetime]  # Returns 'y'
map[pl.Datetime(time_unit='us')]  # KeyError!

```

This behaviour stems from the fact that some dtypes are instantiated objects (mostly the ones that take arguments like `Datetime` and `List`), while others are uninstantiated (like `Int64`).

I think this is actually quite easy to fix: we should always work with instantiated DataType objects. If users specify a dtype input for e.g. a `Series`, we will instantiate it. `Series.dtype` will always return an instantiated object. `isinstance` will always work.

I only see benefits of this approach. But I'm sure the current setup is in place for a reason. Happy to get some feedback on this proposal!
comments:
I was thinking along the same lines, but I'd go even further :)

Have all of the individual dtypes (consistently instantiated, as suggested) live off a single `DType` (or other name ;) class, essentially as properties (so you could refer to them as `DType.Utf8`, `DType.Datetime`, etc ). Implementing a `__call__` would let you refer to them as we do now (eg: `Datetime` vs `Daytime('us')` for convenience, while always really being instantiated. In this model `DType` is not actually a base class for the other types; it's more of a scaffold upon which the "real" types (with their same original base class) live.

This gets us autocomplete for all available types (which we don't really have now), and can easily support discoverable references to _groups_ of types such as `DType.NUMERIC` or `DType.TEMPORAL`, which is also something we don't offer at the moment - and which comes up semi-regularly (most often in reference to type-based selection).

This is a model I have developed previously to great effect. (To give you an idea of the potential scope, I currently have a single master/abstract Type at my current shop that can act as a superset of SQL, Polars, Pandas, Numpy, SQLAchemy, Arrow, and Python types _and_ allow ad-hoc translation/inference to/from them, along with utility functions for classifying supertypes, sorting magnitude of related types, and so on...) 

I'd be happy to build out something similar in Polars (which, as it doesn't need to be so multilingual could be much more targeted than what I've had to develop here ;)

Can also maintain simple references in the `datatypes` module for backwards compatibility, eg: `Utf8 >> DType.Utf8`, and so on, to make any such transition relatively painless.
The difference if instantiated and non-instantiated dtypes was also a problem from string_repr in glimpse: https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/pull/6298

I discussed this with Ritchie, and he's on board with this idea!

> Have all of the individual dtypes (consistently instantiated, as suggested) live off a single `DType` (or other name ;) class, essentially as properties (so you could refer to them as `DType.Utf8`, `DType.Datetime`, etc ).

I think this is a layer of complexity that is not really necessary. I wouldn't want Polars users to type `pl.DType.Utf8`; yes, it will offer autocompletion, but it's also very verbose.

I think we can achieve everything we would want to by having a `DataType` hierarchy with superclasses/subclasses, and actually instantiating the classes. We actually already have such a hierarchy, but it doesn't really work well due to the instantiating issue.

I'm going to take a stab at a PR sometime during the coming weeks, and then we can take it from there.

> I think this is a layer of complexity that is not really necessary. I wouldn't want Polars users to type `pl.DType.Utf8`; yes, it will offer autocompletion, but it's also very verbose.

Agreed; I think our case at work is actually a little different - more of a _"one ring to rule them all"_ scenario, given the multiplicity of supported backends - which works well for us there, but I think you're right that we don't need it here :)

review_comments: We use `call0()` to instantiate the `Int8` class.
Instances of `Int8` can be converted into the corresponding Rust datatype.
